AMAECHI SAYS NIGERIANS, NOT TINUBU, ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE COUNTRY'S PROBLEMS - WHO REALLY BEARS THE RESPONSIBILITY?

By The Insight Lens Project Political Intelligence Desk

Rotimi Amaechi, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice-presidential candidate, has stirred political debate by declaring that Nigerians, rather than President Bola Tinubu, are responsible for the country's problems amid prevailing economic hardship. He has urged citizens to take responsibility by voting against Tinubu in the 2027 general elections.

Amaechi's argument raises an important question about political accountability. While Nigerians have a responsibility to choose their leaders wisely, hold them accountable and participate in democratic processes, they cannot be held responsible for every policy decision or economic outcome of the government they elect.

The argument, however, becomes more complicated when viewed against the realities of governance. Citizens elect governments, but elected leaders make policy decisions, manage public resources and bear responsibility for the consequences of their administration. Rising living costs, unemployment, insecurity and economic pressures cannot simply be transferred to voters because they elected a particular president. Democratic accountability must work both ways.

Interestingly, Amaechi's position also invites scrutiny of his own political history. He was a prominent member of the APC-led political movement that defeated an incumbent government in 2015, served as Minister of Transportation under Muhammadu Buhari and is now seeking power under the ADC. His experience in government makes it reasonable to ask what lessons he has drawn from the policies and decisions of the administrations in which he participated.

Nevertheless, his central message about electoral accountability is worth separating from the controversy surrounding his choice of words. Nigerians have the constitutional right to retain or replace their leaders through elections. But opposition politicians seeking public trust must go beyond blaming voters or criticising the incumbent. They must explain what they would do differently, how they would finance their promises and how their proposed policies would improve the lives of ordinary Nigerians. Ultimately, 2027 should be about accountability for both those who seek to retain power and those who seek to replace them.
